title: Isolation of Patients
path: Prevention and Control of Communicable Diseases

headings.title: Introduction and Principles of Patient Isolation
headings.content: Patient isolation is a foundational strategy in infection prevention and control. It involves separating a client who has a communicable disease from others to interrupt the chain of infection. In Nigerian healthcare settings, where infectious diseases such as Lassa fever, tuberculosis, and cholera present frequent challenges, understanding isolation protocols is vital for clinical safety. The core principle relies on breaking the chain at the portal of exit or mode of transmission, protecting uninfected patients, healthcare personnel, and visitors alike from acquiring nosocomial pathogens.

headings.title: Standard Precautions versus Transmission-Based Precautions
headings.content: Infection control rests on a dual-tier framework. **Standard precautions** form the first tier and apply to the care of all patients regardless of their diagnosed or presumed infection status. They treat all body fluids, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes as potential sources of infection. Conversely, **transmission-based precautions** are tailored for patients known or suspected to be infected with pathogens transmitted by airborne, droplet, or contact routes. These require targeted interventions that go beyond routine hand hygiene and glove use.

headings.title: Categories of Transmission-Based Precautions
headings.content:
Transmission-based precautions are divided into three distinct categories based on how pathogens travel from a source to a susceptible host:

- **Contact Precautions**: Used for infections spread by direct skin-to-skin contact or contact with environmental surfaces (e.g., *C. diff*, multidrug-resistant organisms). Requires gloves and gowns.
- **Droplet Precautions**: Used for pathogens transmitted through large respiratory droplets generated during coughing, sneezing, or talking (e.g., influenza, pertussis). Requires a surgical mask within close range.
- **Airborne Precautions**: Used for tiny droplet nuclei that remain suspended in the air over long distances (e.g., tuberculosis, measles, varicella). Requires a fitted N95 respirator and a negative pressure isolation room.

headings.title: Selection and Sequencing of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
headings.content:
Donning and doffing PPE correctly prevents self-contamination. The sequence for putting on items prioritizes protecting the body first, while removal follows a sequence designed to handle the most contaminated items last or first depending on the specific protocol, ensuring hands remain clean. 

| Action | Correct Sequence | Rationale |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Donning** | Gown $ightarrow$ Mask/Respirator $ightarrow$ Goggles/Face Shield $ightarrow$ Gloves | Pulls cuffs over wrists and ensures respiratory protection seals before touching potentially infected surfaces |
| **Doffing** | Gloves $ightarrow$ Goggles/Face Shield $ightarrow$ Gown $ightarrow$ Mask/Respirator | Removes highest-risk items first to minimize exposure to mucous membranes and skin |

Hand hygiene must be performed between every single step of doffing.

headings.title: Environmental Engineering and Isolation Room Design
headings.content: The physical environment plays a silent yet active role in containing pathogens. Isolation rooms utilize specialized ventilation systems to control airflow direction. **Negative pressure rooms** (airborne infection isolation rooms) ensure that air flows inward from the hallway into the room, preventing infectious particles from drifting into public corridors when doors open. Conversely, **positive pressure rooms** are designed for immunocompromised patients, such as those undergoing bone marrow transplants; air flows outward from the room to keep external contaminants away from the vulnerable occupant.

headings.title: Psychosocial Impact and Patient Rights in Isolation
headings.content: Physical isolation often triggers profound psychological distress. Confined patients frequently experience anxiety, depression, sensory deprivation, and feelings of stigmatization, particularly during major outbreak responses. Healthcare providers must balance infection control demands with fundamental human rights. Patients retain the right to informed consent, respectful communication, and adequate emotional support. Simple nursing interventions—such as frequent verbal check-ins through intercoms or windows, transparent explanations of why precautions are necessary, and facilitating virtual communication with family—help mitigate isolation-induced trauma.

headings.title: Community Health Nursing and Outbreak Management
headings.content: Beyond the acute hospital ward, community health nurses extend isolation principles into primary healthcare centers and rural communities. In resource-constrained settings, home-based care isolation requires creative problem-solving, such as establishing dedicated sick rooms within residential homes and educating family caregivers on safe disposal of infectious waste. Contact tracing, health education, and early identification of suspected cases are vital community nursing functions that stop epidemics before they overwhelm regional health structures.
